newsitem.title: INDONESIA: East Timor violence mars Indonesian election.
newsitem.headline: East Timor violence mars Indonesian election.

text.p: Millions of Indonesians voted on Thursday in the world's fourth most populous nation as police reported 14 deaths in rebel efforts to disrupt the elections in the troubled territory of East Timor.
East Timor police chief Colonel Yusuf Muharam said a soldier guarding a polling booth was shot dead on Thursday, bringing to 14 the number of deaths in the territory since Wednesday night.

Nearly 125 million eligible voters had six hours in which to cast their ballots before the polls closed at 2 p.m. (0700 GMT) in the national and local elections across the archipelago sprawled 5,000 km (3,000 miles) along the equator.
Counting started at individual polling stations, but the ruling Golkar was assured of a comfortable victory.
"It seems to have been very calm and orderly," one senior Asian diplomat said, adding it appeared Golkar could be headed for a landslide in Jakarta.
Golkar won 68 percent of the overall vote in the last elections in 1992 and was seeking just more than 70 percent this time round.

Political analysts said there was concern that supporters of Golkar's main rival during the campaign, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP), might stage protests if they did not increase their share and felt cheated.

The only other party legally entitled to contest the polls, the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), was badly split in a leadership battle and virtually sidelined during the campaign.
Markets shrugged off the election in slow trade, with the rupiah stable at 2,441.50 to the dollar and the stock market index jumping two percent on blue chip buying.
The East Timor police chief, Muharam, said police had shot dead four rebels in a clash in the centre of Dili on Wednesday night during an attempt to disrupt the elections.
He said rebels shot dead at least seven civilians in the town of Los Palos and two in Baucau in separate attacks on Wednesday as opponents of the government destroyed a number of polling booths.

The rebels are fighting Indonesian rule in East Timor after Jakarta invaded the territory in 1975 and incorporated it as its 27th province the following year. The move has never been recognised by the United Nations.

President Suharto, who urged people on Wednesday night to exercise their democratic right and duty by voting, cast his ballot at a polling booth in a garden 250 metres (yards) from his central Jakarta residence.
His eldest daughter Siti Hardyanti Rukmana, one of seven chairmen of Golkar, said after being asked if the party was likely to achieve its 70 percent aim: "I hope so, yes."

The East Timor shootings followed the most violent election campaign in three decades, which ended last Friday with more than 120 deaths in a riot and shopping mall fire in the South Kalimantan capital of Banjarmasin.
Indonesians voted to elect 425 members to the 500-seat House of Representatives and to regional and local assemblies. The other 75 parliamentary seats are filled by the military which does not vote.
But political analysts say the key election is next March when President Suharto, 75, is widely expected to run for a seventh five-year term.
There is keen interest in who he will approve as a running mate, who could be a potential successor.
